articles.title: Rob Lowe Says He ‘Hunkered Down’ and Was Advised to ‘Not Defend Myself’ amid 1988 ‘Sex Tape’ Scandal
articles.summary: The actor revisits the moment he realized the gravity of the situation
articles.body:
As Rob Lowe's star rose in the 1980s, the actor enjoyed documenting his life on video using a video camera

When one of his videos — a sex tape with two women, one of whom he later learned was underage — was exposed, the actor feared his career might be over

The actor shares more about that moment and others in his career in the new documentary, Rob Lowe: The Outsider

Rob Lowe loved documenting his life, but didn't consider how the new technology could backfire.

The actor, 62, talks about his love for the video camera when it was first introduced in Netflix's Rob Lowe: The Outsider , saying that commercially available camcorders were "revolutionary for me."

"The notion that you could have a camera wherever you went. It was great. I documented the Atlanta Braves game, going to the airport, anything and everything. If I was doing it, I was filming it," Lowe said.

"I did a big press tour for About Last Night , all through Europe. I filmed everything. It was amazing to be able to to document everything you're doing in your life and a lot of what I was doing was in bed," he explained.

Lowe goes on to explain that his next project after his summer in Europe was Illegally Yours , which was directed by Peter Bogdanovich. The unconventional process behind the film left the actor with questions about the final product, but he didn't dare question the process. When the studio pulled the plug during filming, he didn't think it would see the light of day.

"But they finished the movie. Ish. This movie was a disaster. It really put me in movie star jail," Lowe explained. "I don't like where my personal life is... where my career is. Nothing comes my way. Nothing's happening. I can't find another movie. That's when I did all this work in politics."

That summer, Lowe began campaigning for Michael Dukakis during the 1988 presidential election and spoke at the Democratic National Convention. Of the time, he recalled, "For me, it was a way to live a different life. People were happy to see me. There's no bad reviews. I was a true believer, the truest of true."

After the campaign, Lowe moved on to his next role in Bad Influence , which reconnected him with Sheryl Berkoff, who would go on to become his wife. Before that, however, a scandal related to Lowe's summer in politics erupted.

"We go to Cannes to announce the movie and it was there that I was told that I was leading the news," he explained. A sex tape showing Lowe engaged with two women, one of whom was just 16 years old while Lowe was 24, became the subject of headlines. Lowe claimed he did not know the girl's age, but was mandated 20 hours of community service in order to avoid more severe legal action. Lowe was not charged with a crime.

As the situation unfolded, Lowe said, "I was advised by Hollywood's finest to not defend myself, so I didn't, because they're the experts."

Of the criminal incident, he said, "I'm not trying to do revisionist history, but we were in over 21 bar. I'm a known film actor and had to show my ID to get in. I had no idea that one of the girls was underage."

"They stole the tape. I knew that there was a possibility that the tape would get out," he claimed. "People would ask me to pay a lot of money to try to keep the tape quiet and I was unwilling to be blackmailed. Well, I showed them, didn't I?"

As the scandal unfolded publicly, Lowe "hunkered down" at home, which concerned brother Chad Lowe. Of the time, Chad recalled, "He was so isolated that I wasn't sure. I just was hearing that it was taking a big toll, and he wasn't taking calls. And that was not normal, to not be able to reach him."

Lowe took the heat, fielding questions about the tape as he promoted Bad Influence and even appearing on Saturday Night Live , ready to poke fun at himself. "And it worked. I was willing to stand in the first and take my slings for a good laugh. And it wasn't meant as a rehabilitation. To me, it was really that I got to host Saturday Night Live , which is something I've been wanting to do forever."

Rob Lowe: The Outsider is now streaming on Netflix.

articles.title: Nacho Cano, contra el PSOE: “Quiero dejar claro cómo actúa esta banda criminal que nos gobierna”
articles.standfirst: El artista habla sobre su detención en ‘Código 10’
articles.summary: El artista habla sobre su detención en ‘Código 10’
articles.body: El caso de Nacho Cano y su detención fue, durante mucho tiempo, uno de los asuntos más polémicos en España. Aquello provocó que muchos rechazaran los proyectos y dieran la espalda a su música debido a sus problemas judiciales. El pasado martes, 24 de noviembre, fue entrevistado en el programa ‘Código 10’ de Cuatro y cargó duramente contra el PSOE de Pedro Sánchez. “Me gustaría dejar muy claro cómo actúa esta banda criminal que nos gobierna y que la gente entienda que soy un ciudadano más, que no he hecho otra cosa que dar puestos de trabajo y que lo que me han hecho a mí se lo podrían hacer a cualquier”, comenzó en su alegato el productor musical. Aseguró Cano que todo el revuelo llegó “por dar 20 becas a unos chavales mexicanos” y que eso le derivó en una escena inesperada: “Me detuvieron por la cara”. “La Audiencia Provincial me ha dado la razón, no he hecho nada malo”, aseveró el artista ante las cámaras del programa de Cuatro. Asimismo, no dudó en hablar sobre la irrupción de tres personas en su casa, llegando incluso a mostrar las imágenes de seguridad, en las que se ve cómo no le robaron, pero sí le movieron las cosas para mandarle un mensaje. Además, compartió el mensaje que mandó a los tres asaltantes: “Quiero saber quién os dio la orden, sé quién fue, pero quiero poder probarlo en un juicio”. “Os ofrezco al que me lo diga, que esté dispuesto a testificar y vean mis abogados que es una prueba real, 50.000 euros. A uno de vosotros tres o a los tres, si queréis decirme quién os dio la orden de que entréis os doy ese dinero”, explicó Nacho Cano en su participación en el programa ‘Código 10’.

articles.title: New movies to watch this weekend: See 'Focker-in-Law' in theaters, rent or buy 'You Can See Everything,' stream 'The Mosquito Bowl' on Netflix
articles.summary: Your guide to the new movies in theaters on Nov. 25 — plus the releases you can catch on streaming.
articles.body:
Want your Thanksgiving dinner with a side of Ben Stiller? His latest Meet the Parents entry — Focker-in-Law , costarring Ariana Grande — is the biggest movie release this Thanksgiving weekend, though I preferred a different sequel that's also out Nov. 25: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , in which David Fincher takes over directing duties from Quentin Tarantino as we revisit Brad Pitt's character from Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood.

At home, you can rent or buy You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's must-see documentary about Elizabeth Holmes that unexpectedly became a box-office sensation, or Wicker, which is sexy, funny and strange.

And on streaming services you're likely already paying for, WWII movie The Mosquito Bowl debuts on Netflix alongside Chris Pratt in Way of the Warrior Kid on Apple TV.

And there's plenty more. Keep reading our latest Trust Me, I Watch Everything to see what's worth watching this Nov. 25 opening weekend.

Why it's a mixed bag: The premise for Focker-in-Law, the fourth film in a franchise with unexpected longevity, practically writes itself.

Ben Stiller is now around the same age that Robert De Niro was when they made Meet the Parents way back in 2000. Naturally, Focker-in-Law sees Stiller's character embodying the role that De Niro played in the original Meet the Parents, a foil to his son's girlfriend, who is now visiting Long Island to, you guessed it, meet the parents.

The twin little Fockers from Little Fockers are all grown up. Henry is played by Skyler Gisondo, who you may recognize from his breakout role this year in Primetime and his viral meme moment , while Beanie Feldstein of Booksmart fame plays Samantha.

The girlfriend who Henry plans to propose to? Ariana Grande's Olivia Jones, a former FBI hostage negotiator, who is introduced in a far-fetched opening sequence that sees Ben Stiller make a fool of himself in a particularly befuddling way on an airplane. It's also exactly the type of nostalgia-fueled legacy sequel to, for example, feature a cameo from the flight attendant from a memorable scene from the original movie.

This is not a series known for its subtlety. Still, in the original Meet the Parents, a very funny movie that still holds up, you could root for Greg, aka Gaylord Focker (get it?!), who was more of a real person at the start than the cartoon character he's become as the franchise progressed. Grande is a fun addition, but the movie never gives her all that much to do.

One aspect of the film that really works is De Niro's Jack Burns, ex-CIA man, fawning over Olivia Jones, ex-FBI agent, infuriating Greg, who is hoping to put Jones through the wringer in the same manner that Jack did to him. Burns's growth into a completely different, self-actualized person, upsetting Greg at every turn, is the funniest running gag in a film that could've used some more of them. De Niro hasn't had this much fun onscreen in ages.

The movie just settles for a low hum of "cute enough" antics instead of either providing some insight into the clash between generations, or at least giving us some wacky set pieces, something the original has in spades…though there is a scene involving cutting in a TSA line that did make me laugh pretty hard.

Focker-in-Law is pretty easily the best movie ever made with Focker in the title, though the bar there is admittedly quite low. The premise is a natural fit and the performers are all game. It's unfortunately just a milder affair than you'd hope for a movie that, should it do well, could help bring the big-budget studio comedy back to movie theaters.

What other critics are saying : Reviews are mixed-negative. William Bibbiani at TheWrap calls it "a painful and pointless experience, which refuses to come to any new conclusions about these characters, other than making them learn the same lessons they already learned years ago." The AP's Mark Kennedy, however, was a fan, writing "You don't need a lie-detector test to know that Grande saves it. She uses her doe-eyed innocence brilliantly... It's very funny and it's exactly the jolt the Focker franchise needed."

How to watch: Focker-in-Law is now playing in theaters nationwide .

Another buzzy release: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth

Why you should see it in a theater: Until this unlikely pairing between two titan filmmakers, a Quentin Tarantino script hasn't been directed by anyone other than Quentin Tarantino since 1996's From Dusk Till Dawn.

David Fincher takes on the Tarantino script in this sort-of sequel to Once Upon a Time in…Hollywood that drops Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton character in favor of following the exploits of his legendary stuntman and one-time best buddy, Cliff Booth, whom Brad Pitt won an Oscar for playing the last time around.

The film, which plays more like a '70s neo-noir than a good vibes buddy hangout movie, is quite funny for a film that gets as pitch-dark as this one does. Cliff Booth, as written in this sequel, is basically a one-size-fits-all fixer for all sorts of Hollywood problems. He's a literary archetype, essentially, and also a movie projectionist and a bartender!

The movie and the character both have a paperback novel quality to them; the idea is that Cliff Booth could star in a dozen of these if one were to pluck one of these nonexistent books off the shelf. Imagine an Elmore Leonard crime caper, and you're halfway there.

Eight years after the events of Once Upon a Time in… Hollywood , Cliff Booth returns to a changing Los Angeles. Now working as a fixer in the shadows of the Hollywood studio system, he finds himself entangled in a dangerous web of secrets, crimes and betrayals that will test everything he knows about loyalty and survival.

Tarantino has insisted that he wants his next film — his 10th — to be his last, but this mystery project has still yet to materialize after his once-planned The Film Critic fell apart. There are sections of Cliff Booth, particularly one monologue from Elizabeth Debicki's character about the merits of movies as art, that feel like they could be lifted from that script. I loved the self-aware meta quality of that debate occurring in this particular movie, which is clearly trying to entertain as genre cinema. But is there more to it?

The cast here is sublime — Debicki is the standout, giving a real Movie Star performance and looking beautiful whilst doing it. I was particularly taken by the decision to have every character she interacts with say a variation of, "Holy s***, you're tall," which is what I imagine interacting with her in real life would be like. Peter Weller (yes, RoboCop himself) is excellent as Cliff's dad, and the dynamic between Weller and Pitt is quite tender and moving, especially if you're familiar with the details of Tarantino's estrangement from his own father. Carla Gugino is dynamite, of course, and Scott Caan is terrific as an annoying movie star.

Pitt has never been better, as effortlessly cool as ever, except for maybe when he played Cliff Booth the last time. What works best is the smoldering romance between him and Debicki. Their dynamic is sexy and funny, the best Tarantino writing of its kind since Jackie Browne.

The meshing of Tarantino's words with Fincher's deliberate and digital aesthetic is jarring at first, and many have deemed it a fundamental mismatch. But I found that it eventually becomes a symphony of violence that feels like a perfect marriage. It's undeniably exciting and fascinating that Fincher and Tarantino made a movie together — that fact is enough to get certain people in seats — and thankfully the final product manages to deliver the specific pleasures of both filmmakers simultaneously.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth may not be the essential, endlessly rewatchable movie that its predecessor is, but it's still well worth seeing it on the big screen, which you fortunately have a chance to do during its IMAX-exclusive run for a couple of weeks before it hits Netflix in December.

What other critics are saying : They're all over the place! Time's Stephanie Zacharek writes, "It's not specific enough to be a movie; it's more of a vibe. But sometimes a vibe is just the ticket, and the movie's affection for a long-lost Los Angeles is probably enough to carry it." Monica Castillo at The AV Club writes, "This follow-up film feels less like a whole story and more like an ellipsis, an unfinished thought meant to leave us wanting more, but which really leaves us feeling like we've been abruptly thrown out of a time machine and back into the modern world."

How to watch: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is now playing in theaters nationwide .

Why it's a disappointment: The latest film from Walt Disney Animation Studios is so generic and familiar that the experience of watching it is best described as feature-length déjà vu. An unconventional teenage girl (Hailee Steinfeld) discovers secret magical abilities which, once unleashed, hurtle her into a vast witch realm called Hexe. Teaming up with her mother (Rashida Jones), she uncovers family mysteries that could change the world of witches forever. It's so "been there, done that" that at a certain point it starts to feel like it's deliberately referencing past Disney things — surely, this enchanted talking book and pen must be an allusion or homage to Beauty and the Beast , for example — rather than just ripping them off, which doesn't make it go down any easier. You're better off watching one of the dozen movies it's reminiscent of than spending money on this one.

How to watch: Hexed is now playing in theaters nationwide .

The buzziest option: You Can See Everything

Why you should watch it: You've likely never seen anything like You Can See Everything , a documentary that plays like a definitive statement on the unknowability of others and how one person's "truth" isn't necessarily … true. It implicates the documentary form itself as inherently manipulative and far from objective, as it attempts to extract honesty and authenticity from disgraced former Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes.

You Can See Everything is the first feature film from Nathan Fielder, a comedian whose nonfiction comedy shows Nathan for You and The Rehearsal function as a twisted form of anthropology as much as they do pure cringe comedy. The film is codirected by Lance Oppenheim, a 30-year-old documentarian whose first non-doc film also just came out: the Chris Hansen movie Primetime .

The logline is this: About a month before she's sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her family's every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss. Fielder himself is featured on camera nearly as much, if not more, than Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, who is a whole other can of worms.

Fielder's awkward and invasive style provides for some wild moments. He and his film crew are actually living at Holmes's house, and there are as many laugh-out-loud bits as there are profoundly unsettling ones. You won't soon forget the beating of some eggs.

Holmes tells Fielder that her extremely literal nature is the cause of the misunderstanding that will soon land her in prison for fraud. A sequence in which Fielder shows her the famous Abbott and Costello "Who's on first?" comedy bit is simultaneously hilarious and illuminating, hands down one of the most memorable scenes I've ever seen in a documentary. Is semiotics really her problem?

The movie evolves into something even more fascinating as Fielder wrestles with Holmes and her insistence that she did absolutely nothing wrong. Ultimately, it seems to be playing with the idea that several things can be true simultaneously.

The action then shifts forward two years and becomes something completely different that people familiar with Fielder's work will instantly recognize: a meta deconstruction of the documentary form and the idea of performance. The less said about the second half, the better, though it is some of the most enthralling cinema I've seen in ages.

You Can See Everything is a brilliant film that feels like it could, and should, become the first documentary ever nominated for Best Picture. It's an incredibly timely document of a post-truth society. The pairing of Fielder, known for his filmic manipulations, and Holmes, a supposed master manipulator now serving time, is a perfect match. You can see everything, but did you?

What other critics are saying: It's one of the best-reviewed movies of the year. AP's Lindsay Bahr aptly sums it up with, "You want something you haven't seen before? Here it is." Amy Nicholson at the Los Angeles Times writes, "The biggest strike against Holmes is this documentary's very existence. Who on Earth would genuinely want Fielder, the human equivalent of a skunk, to crash their last moments with their loved ones as he does his darnedest to stink up the place?"

How to watch: You Can See Everything is now available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

This review was written by my colleague Kelsey Weekman .

Why you should watch it: Part Bridgerton and part dark fairy tale, Wicker is about an enigmatic middle-aged fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who asks a basket weaver (Peter Dinklage) to make her a husband out of wicker. She's not too concerned with the pageantry of marriage in her small medieval farming town, where all men are known by their profession and women are known by their husbands, but she harbors a secret, worldly desire for something more. The basket weaver obliges, and she marries Alexander Skarsgård's basket man, complete with woven muscles and real human eyes, whose work around the house and constant satiation of her carnal desires make all the townsfolk jealous.

The moan-filled trailer went viral in July, inspiring people ( and brands ) to unite in their thirst for a nice basket guy and muse about what women truly want from their relationships. It turned Wicker into a cultural phenomenon; you could take photos with a Wicker cutout and see the movie in a multisensory 4DX screening .

It's hard for anything to live up to so much hype, but I'm thrilled to say that the movie accomplished exactly what it set out to do. There's a lot of pleasure, both physical and emotional, as Skarsgård's basket man repeatedly breaks the bed — and repeatedly fixes it — while saying things like, "I was made to be with you."

The portrayal of this patriarchal society is a bit on the nose at times: Women gleefully lock their necks in a collar during their wedding ceremonies, and they're all vengefully jealous of this wicker guy who actually does housework, and so on. Sometimes it feels like the movie is aggressively pointing out aspects of modern life that still feel antiquated and oppressive, but sometimes you really do just want a man to set societal expectations aside, fix a leaky roof and make you feel good, just for the love of the game.

The wicker man isn't just a hunk who does chores. He absolutely adores the fisherwoman. In one scene, she confesses she doesn't know how to dance as the couples around them do complicated but goofy routines in the town square. But he lovingly and gently holds her as they sway, making everyone else seethe with envy. I was genuinely struck by the sentimental bangers the wicker man whispers to the fisherwoman, like, "Without you … I would never have seen the sun on the ocean or the clouds in the sky."

Make no mistake: There's a lot of sex in this movie, which stands out in a time when so many movies and TV shows cut sex scenes to avoid spooking prudish audiences. But this film has very little nudity, which makes it feel less about the look of sex than the feeling of it. It's about desire, not objectification. I loved that.

The initial clichés of the premise that reeled me in were all subverted by the end, thanks in part to clever writing, but also to the acting masterclass put on by Colman (an Oscar-winning acting heavyweight turned indie darling) and Skarsgård (one of the hottest weird little freak actors in human history). Wicker feels so original and clever that it earns its mushiness. And it's hot.

What other critics are saying: They're enamored! Richard Lawson at the Hollywood Reporter calls it "a warming, sometimes poignant pleasure, a film full of lively personality and possessed of a rather humane outlook on our petty foibles. It is not exactly forgiving, though; the movie has a harder, more merciless edge than one might expect." Amy Nicholson of the Los Angeles Times found it "funny and sexy" but found fault with the film's second half: "The fisherwoman's love story is Wicker 's pulse, but the movie is really about the town, and it sidelines her character to skewer the place."

How to watch: Wicker is now available to rent or buy on Apple TV, Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

What to know: It's not entirely fair to compare The Social Network to its sequel, The Social Reckoning, which dives into the whistleblowing surrounding the Facebook Files . But the movie's complete lack of visual style and embarrassingly generic score are, unfortunately, constant reminders that director David Fincher and the Nine Inch Nails boys are nowhere to be found this time. Instead, the new movie is written and directed by Aaron Sorkin, a case study in the impact a talented director has on a film, even when the writer brings a lot to the table. Ultimately, it feels like a cheap knockoff TV movie follow-up that lacks the verve of the original. ( Read my full review here .)

How to watch: Available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

What to know: An ingenious premise and a terrific lead performance really make Breeder stand out from similar low-budget indie horror fare. An eccentric poodle breeder (Dot-Marie Jones) lures a broke college student to her remote ranch with a promise of research funding. He soon learns that there's a catch. The twist is best discovered in real time, so let's just say this woman is actually interested in breeding more than just animals.

What to know: This act of provocation in the shape of a movie could be the start of a new genre: rage-bait cinema. The Gheorghius, a devout Romanian Norwegian couple, resettle in a village set in a distant fjord where they become close to their neighbors. Their children bond despite their different upbringings. When young Elia Gheorghiu shows up at school with some bruises on her body, the community asks itself if the traditional education that the Gheorghiu children get from their parents has anything to do with it. It's a movie, essentially, about bureaucratic overreach from the state that's overbearing to a comical degree, and it's simply too slanted in one direction to be perceived as neutral or a "both sides make good points" incitement. It's a hell of a conversation starter, though, and features great performances from Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve. The fjord is also quite lovely to look at.

Why you should watch it: Peter Berg, director of several war and action flicks as well as the Friday Night Lights movie, is the perfect director for The Mosquito Bowl, a harrowing war movie that's framed around a football game.

In the aftermath of Pearl Harbor, four college football stars (played by Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson and Tom Francis) enlist in the Marines, discovering the strength of brotherhood and the cost of war.

It's one of the most visceral war movies I've ever seen, with a large chunk of its runtime dedicated to extended battle sequences that are as brutal as any you've ever seen. It's like that iconic sequence from Saving Private Ryan, but throughout. These young men die horrible deaths in front of one another, and you feel the sheer horror of being in that situation, with body parts flying around you that belonged to dear friends of yours.

The problem with the movie is that when it's not putting the viewer right in the middle of harrowing warfare, it's pretty thin. These characters are more archetypes than actual people and the structure of the movie offers them little opportunity for characterization.

The material aims to connect the pastime of football to the experience of war, but it never really makes it clear, other than the general concept of brotherhood and the need to rely on each other as teammates. As a backdrop for a story about a particular group of young men who died in the war, the football setting works well. It just doesn't go as deep as you'd hope.

The Mosquito Bowl delivers the carnage one expects from a war movie in spades, and it's all well crafted by journeyman director/actor Berg, who does also appear in a small role.

What other critics are saying : Reviews are pretty brutal. Robert Abele at the Los Angeles Times says, "I've never been more ready for a football game to be cinematically stirring, and more disappointed that it amounted to a supercut." Though A drian Horton at The Guardian is more on my side, writing, "As with every war movie, there are a thousand possibly better or more challenging war movies existing at the margins of this one. But this one, firmly for the marines, is what we got."

How to watch: The Mosquito Bowl is now streaming on Netflix .

Another buzzy option: Way of the Warrior Kid

Why you should skip it: Way of the Warrior Kid certainly means well, but its cartoonish approach is rather unconvincing, and it winds up feeling like military propaganda for children.

Jake (Chris Pratt) is an injured Navy SEAL who becomes a mentor for his shy, struggling nephew Marc (Jude Hill). Using the principles of his military training, Jake teaches Marc how to be a Warrior Kid as he enters high school. Essentially, Chris Pratt "Queer Eyes" the kid with a life makeover, but with the added bonus of teaching children about the potential benefits of the U.S. military.

Even something simple like the kid being bullied in this movie is rendered ridiculous and hard to believe. At school, with teachers in earshot and present, these kids are horrible to him, and nobody says a thing. It's all just pitched up that high so everything comes off like an after-school special. Don't even get me started on the outrageous third-act set piece.

It's meant to be a schmaltzy feel-good time, but it's just too by-the-numbers to get behind, playing like a first-draft script without the necessary additions to make it work. Chris Pratt sleepwalks through it, phoning it in because it's the same type of character he always plays, and he also takes away focus from the true lead of the film, which should be the kid but sort've isn't. Way of the Warrior Kid is cliché-ridden generic cinema at its least subtle.

What other critics are saying : Reviews are pretty bad so far. Variety's Todd Gilchrist writes that it "doesn't bring enjoyment, empowerment or enlightenment, so much as a sense of, 'Okay, that happened.'" The AV Club's Andy Crump correctly points out that Chris Pratt gets in his own way.

How to watch: Way of the Warrior Kid is now streaming on Apple TV .

We'll see you next Friday for the Dec. 4 opening weekend.

articles.title: 'O Saathi Re' trailer: Imtiaz Ali explores love, marriage and complicated relationships in Aditi Rao Hydari, Arjun Rampal series
articles.summary: Imtiaz Ali is back with a new love story, but this time, the focus is on a marriage falling apart and three people caught in complicated relationships.
articles.body: Imtiaz Ali is back with a new love story, but this time, the focus is on a marriage falling apart and three people caught in complicated relationships.The trailer of his upcoming series ‘O Saathi Re’, starring Aditi Rao Hydari, Avinash Tiwary and Arjun Rampal, was unveiled on Tuesday. The series is set to premiere on Netflix on December 4.The trailer introduces viewers to Roshni (Aditi Rao Hydari) and Karan (Avinash Tiwary), whose married life is going through a difficult phase. Things become more complicated when Roshni develops feelings for Pradyuman (Arjun Rampal). As the three find themselves caught in an emotional situation, the story looks at love, marriage, personal choices and the difficulty of letting go.While Karan continues to love Roshni, she finds herself trying to understand her feelings and what she wants from life. Pradyuman, meanwhile, brings a different perspective into her life. The series looks at whether love is about holding on to someone or allowing them to make their own choices.Take a look View this post on InstagramA post shared by Netflix India (@netflix_in)Aditi Rao Hydari, who plays Roshni, spoke about portraying a woman trying to understand her own identity while dealing with her relationships. As per a release, she said, “ Roshni is a woman trying to understand herself beyond the roles she has always played in other people’s lives. She is a daughter, a wife and a sister, but beneath all of that is an individual with her own desires, contradictions and vulnerabilities. What I loved about her was that she isn’t perfect or easy to define.Arjun Rampal, who plays Pradyuman, spoke about his character’s place in Roshni’s life and how he changes the dynamics of the story. He said, “ Pradyuman brings a very different energy into Roshni’s world. He is confident, self-assured and sees her beyond the identities she has always been associated with.”Created, written and showrun by Imtiaz Ali, ‘O Saathi Re’ is directed by Arif Ali. The series also explores issues such as personal choices, expectations in relationships and the difference between love and attachment.Produced by Window Seat Films, the series is produced by Imtiaz Ali, Mohit Choudhary and Shibasish Sarkar. ‘O Saathi Re’ will premiere on Netflix on December 4, 2026.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Arushi Nishank breaks silence on alleged link-up rumours with Union Minister Chirag Paswan
articles.summary: Actress and producer Arushi Nishank, daughter of former Uttarakhand Chief Minister Ramesh Pokhriyal Nishank, has addressed the social media speculation
articles.body: Actress and producer Arushi Nishank, daughter of former Uttarakhand Chief Minister Ramesh Pokhriyal Nishank, has addressed the social media speculation linking her with Union Minister Chirag Paswan.She clarified that the two share a good friendship. Speaking to IANS, Arushi said that a meeting with Chirag, during which she gifted him a book to congratulate him, was apparently misinterpreted and led to rumors about their alleged wedding."What can I say about myself? I am troll material. Just look at me; I can get trolled anytime. But jokes apart, Chirag is a very good friend of mine, and he is doing really well. I had gone to congratulate him by gifting him a book, which apparently turned into a wedding card. So, I would say that's one of the disadvantages of being a public figure," she told IANS.Arushi also spoke about facing negative comments on social media following her meeting with Bageshwar Dham's Maharaj ji. She said the remarks saddened her, particularly because they involved a religious figure whom she holds in high regard."I had also met our Maharaj ji of Bageshwar Dham, and people made very nasty comments on that too, and I was reading them. My heart was saddened because he is a saintly person, and saying such things is not right. But it's okay, I think we have gotten better now," she added.Arushi's remarks come amid ongoing social media speculation about her association with Chirag Paswan. The dating rumours gained momentum after Arushi shared pictures with Chirag Paswan on social media during her visit to his residence. A book that she had gifted him was also reportedly mistaken for a wedding invitation, further fuelling speculation about their relationship.As per her social media profile, Arushi is an actress, film producer, trained Kathak dancer and TEDx speaker. articles.title: Sooraj Barjatya admits he let Hrithik Roshan, Kareena Kapoor and Abhishek Bachchan down with 'Main Prem Ki Diwani Hoon': 'It became my biggest teacher'
articles.summary: Filmmaker Sooraj Barjatya has honestly looked back at his 2003 romantic drama 'Main Prem Ki Diwani Hoon', confessing that he felt guilty about not doing
articles.body: Filmmaker Sooraj Barjatya has honestly looked back at his 2003 romantic drama 'Main Prem Ki Diwani Hoon', confessing that he felt guilty about not doing justice to its leading trio, Hrithik Roshan, Kareena Kapoor Khan and Abhishek Bachchan. He explained how chasing market trends shaped the film and how the experience changed his way of working.Sooraj Barjatya on 'Main Prem Ki Diwani Hoon'Speaking to Variety India while promoting his upcoming release 'Yeh Prem Mol Liya', the director shared why the film still weighs on his mind. He said, "I had Hrithik, Abhishek, Kareena and I felt that I had let them down in a big way. I made that film according to the way I thought the commercial demands of the time were moving. But it became my biggest teacher. It taught me that I should do what I know and what I genuinely like."Film finds new fansAlthough the movie did not click the way he hoped, it has slowly won over a younger generation of viewers who are watching it years after its theatrical run. Sooraj Barjatya said he is delighted by this change. He said, "When I see younger audiences discovering the film and enjoying it, I feel very happy. It has found its own audience and its own place in popular culture."About 'Main Prem Ki Diwani Hoon'The 2003 film was helmed by Barjatya and led by Hrithik, Kareena and Abhishek. Pankaj Kapur, Himani Shivpuri and Reema Lagoo played key supporting characters in the romantic drama.What's next for Sooraj BarjatyaSooraj Barjatya is now preparing to bring his next directorial, 'Yeh Prem Mol Liya', to cinemas. It will be his first big-screen outing since 'Uunchai' (2022). The family entertainer features Ayushmann Khurrana and Sharvari in the lead, with Ayushmann playing the beloved character of Prem. articles.title: Dave Bautista's inspiring journey: How he overcame childhood poverty, financial struggles and WWE challenges to become a wrestling legend and respected Hollywood star
articles.summary: Discover how Dave Bautista transformed his life from childhood poverty and financial struggles to become a WWE legend and successful Hollywood actor, overcoming numerous challenges along the way.
articles.body: Dave Bautista’s road to stardom was no ordinary journey, and before he became a Hollywood staple and one of WWE’s most recognizable performers. Also, he was struggling financially and dealing with family issues and an uncertain future in Washington, D.C. His challenging childhood motivated him to build a new life.Bautista’s opportunity came relatively late in life, as opposed to many wrestlers who enter the industry in their teens, and his journey involved juggling multiple jobs, facing professional rejection, and ultimately taking big risks to chase opportunities beyond the wrestling ring.How Dave Bautista overcame childhood struggles to become a WWE legendDave Bautista grew up in difficult financial conditions and an unstable environment, and he grew up in Washington, D.C., a place where neighborhood violence was common and daily life was difficult to navigate. He also lacked confidence and often felt awkward in social situations.It became a big outlet in bodybuilding. As a teenager, he started weightlifting and found confidence and discipline from the regular training. The gym was there for him when his future was uncertain.More problems came with his early adulthood. Bautista left school at 17 and became a nightclub bouncer. He’d been in the profession for more than ten years, earning enough to live on from one day to the next but found it hard to create any long-term financial security.A particularly tough Christmas was a turning point. He was unable to afford presents for his two daughters and had to borrow money from his employer. The experience caused him to think about an entirely different career. Now in his early 30s, he decided to become a professional wrestler with no experience in the industry.Dave Bautista turned WWE success into Hollywood opportunitiesDave Bautista's professional wrestling career was not without its ups and downs. He was cut from his first tryout for World Championship Wrestling (WCW), but kept training and eventually wound up in WWE’s developmental system. Afa Anoaʻi trained him at his Wild Samoan Training Center and taught him the technical skills he would need to wrestle professionally.In 2002, he debuted on the WWE main roster as Deacon Batista, before becoming known simply as Batista. Being in Evolution with Triple H, Ric Flair and Randy Orton helped cement him as a big-time player. His strong presence and growing popularity would eventually see him become a six-time world champion, with major wins over existing WWE stars.But wrestling wasn’t the only business Bautista wanted to be in. He has had a successful career in the ring and is now taking his talents to the acting world. He spent some time early in his career in smaller films and TV projects, giving him some experience beyond pro wrestling.The biggest turning point was his decision to leave WWE in 2010. Bautista sought more chances to develop as an actor, even if it meant walking away from a successful career and a consistent paycheck from professional wrestling.Dave Bautista overcame financial struggles to earn respectDave Bautista’s move to Hollywood wasn’t without its financial obstacles, at least initially. After he departed from WWE, he had trouble landing any major acting roles and eventually squandered most of the money he made in his wrestling career. His house was foreclosed, and he sold many valuable possessions to try to get his finances back in order.Dave Bautista didn't take every action role that paid and instead chose to focus on developing his acting skills. He worked with acting coaches and took smaller jobs in Los Angeles while waiting for the right opportunities to present themselves.He broke through in 2014 starring as Drax the Destroyer in Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy. The role brought him to a much larger international audience and helped establish him in the film industry.The success of the Marvel franchise opened the door for more challenging projects. Dave Bautista would go on to appear in Blade Runner 2049, Dune, Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery, and Knock at the Cabin. These performances showed he could move beyond the physically demanding action roles and try more emotionally layered characters.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Brad Pitt, Angelina Jolie Call It Quits on Years-long Legal Saga, Settle Case That Led to Abuse Claims
articles.summary: After the 'Cliff Booth' star sued in 2022 to stop Jolie from selling her stake in winery Château Miraval, the actress revealed accusations of abuse during an...
articles.body:
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running dispute over the sale of their French winery, a lawsuit that opened the door for the actress to accuse her ex-husband of abusing her and their children.

Both sides on Wednesday moved to dismiss claims against each other. Terms of the settlement weren't disclosed.

"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said representatives for Jolie and Pitt in a statement. "Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us."

The couple purchased the 1,200-acre winery in the South of France where they married, Château Miraval, in 2008. Jolie planned to sell her half to Pitt in the wake of their divorce, court filings alleged, until negotiations broke down over his insistence that she sign a nondisclosure agreement barring her from publicizing allegations of abuse leading up to their split.

Jolie balked at the ask and instead struck a $64 million deal with billionaire alcohol magnate Yuri Shefler for her half of the winery. Pitt in 2022 filed a lawsuit, claiming that the actress reneged on an unwritten agreement that they wouldn't sell their stakes in the business without the other's consent. That led to a countersuit from Jolie publicizing for the first time abuse allegations against Pitt in a 2016 altercation on a private plane in which she claimed that the actor "grabbed her by the head and shook her," "choked one of the children" and "struck another in the face."

At the time, a representative for Pitt denied the allegations. Jolie "continues to rehash, revise and reimagine her description of an event that happened 6 years ago by adding completely untrue information each time she fails to get what she wants," the spokesperson said. "Her story is constantly evolving."

Wednesday's settlement ends a contentious case that peeled back the origins of Pitt and Jolie's divorce and hostility between the former couple. Pitt continues to pursue claims against Shefler, who allegedly orchestrated the acquisition in secret alongside Jolie, and Shefler's company Tenute del Mondo, the wine arm of the Stoli Group. The actor seeks a court order allowing him to purchase Jolie's shares in Miraval at the same valuation Shefler acquired them, plus unspecified damages.

A state appeals court earlier this year found that Shefler played a vital role in structuring and finalizing the deal to purchase Miraval. It pointed to him guaranteeing $39 million of the purchase using his own funds, a provision he wouldn't agree to if he wasn't involved in the agreement. Shefler sent three letters to Jolie over the course of the transaction, according to court filings. One thanked her for accepting his offer and assured her that a deal would be made "despite personal complications." Another asked Jolie to postpone paying an installment on the purchase due to complications with Pitt.

Since the allegations became public in 2022, Pitt has continued starring in major studio productions, like F1 and Heart of the Beast , maintaining his dual-standing as one of Hollywood's most bankable leading men and a prolific producer of prestige film through Plan B Entertainment. Jolie, meanwhile, momentarily took a step back from acting before earning critical acclaim for her portrayal as Maria Callas in Maria .

In her cross complaint, Jolie detailed a physical altercation with Pitt, with him on one side and her and their children on the other.

"Pitt lunged at his own child and Jolie grabbed him from behind to stop him," the complaint stated. "To get Jolie off his back, Pitt threw himself backwards into the airplane's seats injuring Jolie's back and elbow. The children rushed in and all bravely tried to protect each other."

At one point, Pitt poured beer on Jolie; at another, he poured beer and wine on the children, the lawsuit alleged. Once the flight landed, Jolie claimed Pitt pushed her when she told him that she and the children were going to a hotel. "He also grabbed and shook Jolie by the head and shoulders, causing one of the children to beg, 'Don't hurt her,'" the complaint stated. "He let Jolie go, but then called her a 'bitch,' before adding, 'Fuck you, fuck you all.'" Jolie filed for divorce five days later.

The FBI investigated the 2016 altercation but declined to press charges. A redacted report on the case stated that the investigating agent found there was probable cause to pursue a criminal case but that charges would not be filed due to " several factors ," according to The New York Times . It described Jolie as being "conflicted on whether or not to be supportive of charges."

Pitt is represented by John Berlinski and Julia Cherlow, partners at Bird Marella, while Jolie was represented by Paul Murphy and Daniel Csillag. Alejandro Brito, who handles media lawsuit for President Trump, represents Shefler.

articles.title: Shane Gillis wishes ex-girlfriend 'the best' after tell-all essay accusing him of cheating and 'red flags'
articles.summary: Comedian Shane Gillis wished ex-girlfriend Grace Brassel "the best" after she published an essay in The Cut alleging cheating and mistreatment during their yearlong romance.
articles.body: Comedian Shane Gillis’ ex-girlfriend wrote a lengthy piece this week about their yearlong relationship, saying his controversial "Saturday Night Live" joke about women at the gym reflects how he treats women behind closed doors. In an essay published by The Cut, content creator Grace Brassel wrote that the comedian pressured her into quitting her job, isolated her from friends and family and cheated on her before their split in August 2025. Speaking to Fox News Digital, Gillis responded to Brassel’s claims, saying, "Grace and I had some good times together. Breakups are tough, and I wish her the best." 'SNL' CAST MEMBER MICHAEL CHE SHRUGS OFF SHANE GILLIS' MONOLOGUE JOKE SAYING, 'THAT'S COMEDY' In a statement to Fox News Digital, Brassel said she wrote the essay to help other women. "I wrote this essay to help other women, and for them to know there is a life past it, these kinds of relationships. The beautiful DMs I am receiving mean so much to me. No matter what age you are, this can happen to you, and I always wished someone could have told me sooner. I hope it can help more girls speak out and stand up for themselves," Brassel said. Brassel referenced Gillis’ recent controversial comments regarding women’s gym attire on "SNL" being that of "whores," writing that she wasn’t the "least bit surprised." "Until last August, I was in a yearlong relationship with Shane, and his comments didn’t faze me. After our time together, how do I think he feels about women? He doesn’t like them much," Brassel wrote. The pair began talking in May 2024 after Brassel sent him direct messages on Instagram, and she initially described their whirlwind romance as a "dream." However, she explained that when they eventually moved in together, it was a "nonstop party," which made it difficult for her to keep up her day job as a social media manager. She claimed Gillis encouraged her to quit, and when they moved to Pennsylvania to shoot his Netflix series "Tires," she felt as though his expectations of her changed. "I felt like I was turning into a 25-year-old housewife, someone who cooked, cleaned, did the laundry, and waited for her man to come home from a long day at work. I never said I was capable of all that, but it felt like an expectation," Brassel wrote. "When things weren’t exactly to his liking, he would tell me that I wasn’t ‘being good.’ You know, the way you would talk to a dog." 'SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE' STAR WOULD SIT SHANE GILLIS DOWN 'LIKE A LITTLE KID' OVER PROVOCATIVE MONOLOGUE She added that she ignored many "red flags," claiming he would say something "remarkably cruel" and play it off as a joke, and noted she felt she needed to start dressing more "conservatively." "I cried every day. I would call my mom in tears, telling her that I didn’t know if I was meant for this life. My six-month free trial of Sweet Shane Gillis had run out, and it was time for me to start paying," she wrote. Brassel alleged that things came to a head on the Fourth of July, when she said she discovered Gillis’ infidelity after going through his phone and finding explicit messages with another woman that had been going on for months. "I scrolled and realized they had been sexting for months and had probably had in-person encounters as well. The floor seemed to give way beneath my feet," she recalled. Brassel admitted she "snapped" when confronting him. She described punching a hole in the bathroom wall and throwing her phone and a chair before the two eventually went through an on-and-off breakup. She claimed they had considered reconciling, but that Gillis said they could never mend things after she began telling others how he treated her. BROADCAST BIAS: FEMINIST FREAKOUT OVER SHANE GILLIS COMMENT IS THE REAL JOKE Brassel added that the outrage over Gillis’ recent monologue on "SNL" gave her "some kind of closure." "He had flown too close to the sun, and people were finally seeing the man I knew. I had spent so long protecting this part of my life, afraid to speak publicly about it, and then he just did it himself. Finally, some initiative," Brassel wrote at the end of the essay. She also addressed the attention the essay has gotten in a video posted to her 124,000 followers on Instagram, saying she’s been working on the essay for a month and was fully aware of the "discourse" it would cause. "I'm well aware of the discourse that was going to happen," Brassel said. "And I weighed out my options, and I think that it is a net positive, no matter what. I can handle the heat. I'm in the kitchen, girl. I can handle the heat." SWIFTIES CLAIM TRAVIS KELCE DID THE UNSPEAKABLE BY LIKING SHANE GILLIS' 'SNL' MONOLOGUE & THEY'RE NOT HAPPY Gillis addressed the controversy he spurred on "SNL," telling host Joe Rogan earlier this month that he had promised the show’s producers "no controversy." "Not to defend ‘SNL,’ they don't approve it. I mean, they could shut it down," Gillis said on "The Joe Rogan Experience." "But you don't write your set and give it to them," he added. "Unless you’re not a comedian. I’m sure non-comics, they write the set for them. They have writers that write the monologue for them." "The funniest part was... they were like, ‘What’s going on with the monologue?’ And I was like, ‘It’s not great, but I don’t say anything bad.’ The whole time, I was like, ‘Fellas, I’m giving you a solid C-minus of a monologue, but I promise there’s no controversy. I’m calling myself fat for f---ing 10 minutes. That’s it.'" Gillis drew criticism from entertainment figures, including actor Dan Levy and former "SNL" cast member Ego Nwodim, after joking during his opening monologue last month that women at gyms "just dress like whores now." The appearance marked his third time hosting the NBC sketch seies, which briefly hired and then fired him in 2019 as a cast member over a podcast appearance where he made jokes deemed offensive. articles.title: Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future
articles.summary: Google is thinking about how generative AI could be used to give people endless feeds of slop entertainment.
articles.body: Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version, and we could see this monstrosity come to market. First spotted by Patentlyze, the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a person’s demographic data and viewing history to create its own prompts that would then be fed into an LLM to help generate AI videos tailored to that person’s specific interests. In addition to factoring in what kinds of videos a user tends to watch, the system would capture contextual data from their device like IP addresses, GPS locations, and specific details about the user’s age. My Channel could also base its prompts on current news like sports scores and things happening on social media, and all of the video generation would take place on Google’s servers. According to the patent, My Channel would be able to churn out entire movies of various genres. If a user watches a lot of videos about Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, the system might serve up something like Ash Koosha’s Odysseus: The Fall. The patent details how My Channel might be able to connect to other streaming services — which would give it even more information about users and, presumably, access to useful training data for video generation. It all seems like a convoluted way to whip up AI knockoffs of professionally produced art, but what’s most unsettling about the patent are its mentions of My Channel creating digital avatars of users and turning them into “the protagonist or lead character” in the content it pumps out. [Image: Setting aside the fact that My Channel would use photos, videos, and audio clips of people to create these avatars, the system sounds like it is designed to generate a form of “entertainment” that is deeply at odds with what makes engaging with art a worthwhile, enjoyable experience. It can be fun to metaphorically project one’s self into fictional narratives to understand how characters feel, but what Google is proposing is giving people access to an endless supply of bespoke content that doesn’t at all encourage them to use their imaginations to empathize with or relate to the characters. The patent makes it seem like Google thinks that viewers would be entertained enough just by seeing themselves onscreen. That’s bleak in and of itself because My Channel sounds very much like an unholy cross between JibJab and the panoptic elements of Google. My Channel feels like an even more depressing idea when you consider how the service would make it that much easier for its users to avoid broadening their horizons by being exposed to new things that exist outside their comfort zones. If Google were able to strike the right licensing deals with other streaming services, My Channel users could presumably gorge themselves on artless AI regurgitations of preexisting content. That might keep some people glued to the service — a goal that every streaming platform strives for — but it would also discourage them from engaging with entertainment that isn’t expressly crafted to appeal to their assumed tastes. When people refer to AI-generated videos as “slop,” they’re talking about the fact that generative models are incapable of generating art with the same kind of creative intention that makes human-made stories compelling. Video generation models can mimic visual elements of the data (read: movies and series) they’re trained on, but they cannot truly think or feel in the way that directors, writers, and actors can. This reality is why it has been so baffling to see AI-boosting entertainment companies, streamers, and studios insisting that the technology will fundamentally revolutionize the industry for the better. It feels much more likely that gen AI is going to keep flooding the internet with garbage no one wants to watch.

articles.title: Andy Taylor, guitarist of new wave icons Duran Duran, dies at 65
articles.summary: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, whose huge pop hits include “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “The Reflex” and “Rio” and whose rise up the charts was inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died.
articles.body: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, whose huge pop hits include “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “The Reflex” and “Rio” and whose rise up the charts was inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65. Taylor’s death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran’s website. “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed,” the band said. On the night he was inducted in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend. “I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band,” he wrote. “You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one’s own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible.” The two-time Grammy Award-winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the UK and 18 in the U.S. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients. The band’s imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as “Girls on Film” and “Union of the Snake” and the moody ballads “The Chauffeur” and “Save a Prayer.” Other hits in the coming years included “The Wild Boys,” “New Moon on Monday” and “Come Undone.” Their popularity was cemented when they recorded the James Bond theme song “A View to a Kill” and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985. Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesizers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band were all over radio and young people’s walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heartthrobs and the band being labeled part of the New Romantics. Princess Diana was known to be a fan and that meant a lot to the band.

articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65; bandmates pay emotional tribute
articles.summary: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor, whose playing powered 1980s hit "Rio" and "Hungry Like the Wolf," has died at age 65 of prostate cancer, his family said.
articles.body: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor has died of prostate cancer at the age of 65, Fox News Digital confirmed. Taylor died peacefully at home surrounded by family on Monday, according to a joint statement from his family and former bandmates. "To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather," his wife, Tracey, said on behalf of the family. "He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home." articles.title: Elena Furiase cuenta cómo Lolita descubrió que había perdido la virginidad: "Ya eres mujer"
articles.standfirst: La actriz madrileña y Marta Hazas han sido las invitadas de Pablo Motos este miércoles en 'El Hormiguero'
articles.summary: La actriz madrileña y Marta Hazas han sido las invitadas de Pablo Motos este miércoles en 'El Hormiguero'
articles.body: 'El Hormiguero' ha cerrado este miércoles la semana con la visita de las actrices Marta Hazas y Elena Furiase, quienes han presentado la película 'Hechos probados', que se estrenó en cines el 20 de noviembre. Se trata de un drama judicial que introduce, por primera vez en España, el género del 'true legal': una propuesta inspirada en casos reales y en la actividad de una 'legaltech', donde se traslada a la ficción conflictos jurídico-cotidianos. PABLO MOTOS. Presentáis 'Hechos probados', que ya está en los cines. Marta, ¿qué historia cuenta la película? MARTA HAZAS. Interpretamos a dos hermanas abogadas que atraviesan momentos vitales muy distintos. Mi personaje, Inés, es una mujer mucho más empática, muy centrada en cuidar a los demás, mientras que su hermana tiene un perfil más ambicioso y más orientado a los negocios. Trabajamos juntas en una legal tech, donde el personaje de Elena es mi jefa. A partir de ahí se desarrollan varios casos basados en hechos reales que vamos resolviendo a lo largo de la película. Mi hermana la interpreta Amaia Salamanca y el conflicto entre ambas tiene mucho peso en la historia. PABLO MOTOS. En la película, el conflicto entre hermanas es importante. Elena, ¿es verdad que tú y tu hermano Guillermo siempre os habéis cubierto las espaldas cuando alguno hacía alguna trastada? ELENA FURIASE. Sí, eso es totalmente cierto. Cuando éramos más jóvenes, nos protegíamos muchísimo. Ahora ya somos mayores y no hacemos tantas locuras, pero cuando pasaba algo, siempre nos ayudábamos. Si uno necesitaba que el otro le sacara de algún apuro, allí estábamos. Lo curioso es que mi madre siempre terminaba enterándose de todo. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Y cómo os descubría Lolita? ELENA FURIASE. Porque tiene una intuición increíble. Siempre digo que mi madre fue el ChatGPT antes de que existiera ChatGPT. Le hacías una pregunta y ya sabía la respuesta antes incluso de que ocurrieran las cosas. Tenía una capacidad asombrosa para leer las situaciones. PABLO MOTOS. De hecho, has contado alguna vez que supo que habías perdido la virginidad sin que le dijeras nada. ELENA FURIASE. Sí, fue exactamente así. Llegué a casa por la mañana después de una noche muy especial y, cuando entré, me pidió que fuera a hablar con ella. Me senté y, sin rodeos, me dijo: "Ya eres mujer". Yo me puse a llorar inmediatamente. Había acertado por completo. Fue un momento muy bonito y muy emocionante. PABLO MOTOS. Elena, en la película aparecen personajes bastante oportunistas. ¿Es cierto que cuando empezabas en esta profesión pensabas que todo el mundo era bueno y terminabas contando tu vida a cualquiera? ELENA FURIASE. Sí, absolutamente. Sigo pensando que la mayoría de la gente es buena, aunque los malos hagan mucho ruido. Cuando empecé, cualquier compañero amable me parecía automáticamente un amigo. Esta profesión puede ser bastante solitaria y yo siempre buscaba refugio en la gente que tenía cerca. Con el tiempo entendí que una persona puede ser encantadora contigo sin que necesariamente forme parte de tu círculo íntimo. No es que haya gente mala, simplemente no todo el mundo tiene el mismo interés o el mismo vínculo contigo. MARTA HAZAS. Yo recuerdo perfectamente conocer a Elena durante El Internado. Estábamos en el Festival de Málaga y me llamó muchísimo la atención su manera de ver el mundo. Me transmitía una enorme nobleza. Pensé que tenía un corazón inmenso y una confianza muy bonita en la gente. PABLO MOTOS. Marta, en una profesión donde hay mucho ego, ¿qué has aprendido de la gente falsa? MARTA HAZAS. He aprendido a ir con orejeras y centrarme en lo mío. No me interesa demasiado perder energía en eso. Sí he vivido situaciones en las que una persona te trata fenomenal en un determinado contexto y, de repente, en otro donde ya no resultas tan interesante, parece que ni te conoce. Al principio duele un poco, pero después entiendes que dice más de la otra persona que de ti. ELENA FURIASE. Y además Marta es exactamente igual siempre. Si te trata con cariño la primera vez, la segunda te trata aún mejor y la tercera mejor todavía. Hemos pasado mucho tiempo sin vernos y cada vez que nos reencontramos siempre ha sido igual de cariñosa conmigo. PABLO MOTOS. Hablando de rarezas, Marta, ¿es cierto que tienes fobia a las estatuas? MARTA HAZAS. Sí, y es una cosa bastante absurda porque ni siquiera la entiendo. Tiene nombre, se llama automatonofobia, pero en mi caso no son los muñecos lo que me da miedo. Me asustan las estatuas gigantes, las esculturas colosales, todo aquello que resulta desmesurado. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Qué sientes exactamente cuando estás delante de una? MARTA HAZAS. Una sensación muy extraña, como si pudiera cobrar vida. Sé que es irracional y me repito constantemente que no va a ocurrir nada, pero hay algo que me paraliza. Me pasa con esculturas enormes, con bustos y hasta con determinadas figuras que aparecen por sorpresa. Lo peor es el factor sorpresa. Entrar en una iglesia, girar una esquina y encontrarme una escultura delante me produce muchísimo rechazo. PABLO MOTOS. ¿La Estatua de la Libertad, por ejemplo? MARTA HAZAS. Horrible. No podría estar cerca. El David de Miguel Ángel también me daría mucho respeto, aunque sea una obra maravillosa. Me gusta el arte y disfruto visitando museos, pero determinadas esculturas me generan una sensación física muy difícil de explicar. PABLO MOTOS. Elena, tú tienes una fobia diferente: las lesiones y las roturas de huesos ELENA FURIASE. Sí, no tanto los huesos en sí como todo lo relacionado con fracturas, luxaciones y lesiones de ese tipo. Si alguien empieza a contarme que se desencajó una rodilla o un hombro, me pongo fatal. Lo pasó realmente mal. PABLO MOTOS. Tanto que durante una mudanza preferiste no acercarte a ayudar a tu pareja cuando se lesionó una rodilla. ELENA FURIASE. Totalmente cierto. Estaba embarazada de mi segunda hija y estábamos haciendo una mudanza. De repente oí un golpe enorme y a mi marido gritar que se había hecho daño en la rodilla. Yo empecé a imaginarme la rótula fuera de sitio y todo tipo de escenarios espantosos. No fui capaz de acercarme porque sabía que me iba a marear. Le pregunté si quería que llamara a su madre o a su hermano, pero no podía enfrentarme a la posibilidad de ver algo relacionado con la lesión. PABLO MOTOS. Marta, también tenéis una costumbre curiosa en casa. Cuando recibís una mala noticia profesional, abrís una botella de champán. MARTA HAZAS. Sí, empezó hace años, cuando estábamos intentando sacar adelante proyectos audiovisuales y recibíamos negativas continuamente. Había épocas en las que todo eran puertas cerradas. Un día teníamos una botella de champán en casa y decidimos abrirla precisamente después de recibir otro "no". Lo hicimos un poco por rebeldía. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Y funcionó? MARTA HAZAS. Nos ayudó a cambiar la perspectiva. Pensamos que cada negativa nos acercaba a algo diferente y probablemente mejor. Desde entonces, cuando aparece una mala noticia, intentamos celebrarla de alguna manera porque significa que toca buscar una nueva oportunidad. PABLO MOTOS. Elena, cambiando de tema, también eres una apasionada de las vajillas. ELENA FURIASE. Sí, lo reconozco abiertamente. Me encantan. Soy una auténtica enamorada de las vajillas bonitas. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Cuántas tienes? ELENA FURIASE. Me gusta encontrar diseños bonitos. No tienen por qué ser carísimas. Puedes encontrar vajillas preciosas en muchos sitios. De hecho, cuando me preguntan qué quiero para Reyes o para mi cumpleaños, muchas veces respondo que una vajilla nueva. Siempre me hace ilusión. PABLO MOTOS. Marta, además de la película, sigues de gira con Un matrimonio sin filtros. MARTA HAZAS. Sí, seguimos con la gira. Cerraremos esta etapa en Santander durante diciembre, pero el próximo año regresaremos a Madrid. Estaremos en el Teatro Alcázar a partir del 11 de febrero, que además coincide con el cumpleaños de Javi, así que tendremos doble motivo para celebrarlo. PABLO MOTOS. Para terminar, ¿qué os gustaría que encontrara el espectador en 'Hechos probados'? MARTA HAZAS. Una historia entretenida, cercana y con personajes muy humanos. ELENA FURIASE. Y también una reflexión sobre la familia, sobre los vínculos y sobre cómo afrontamos los problemas desde puntos de vista muy distintos. Creo que el público puede sentirse muy identificado con las dos hermanas.

articles.body:
Leo Tomassini lança em 1º de dezembro o single 'Claro da lua', gravado com Guinga — Foto: Fernanda Vogas / Divulgação

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

♬ “Escuta comigo o claro da lua / Valsa comigo a valsa do nada / Me dê a mão, me dê a mão / Vamos flutuar no azul”, convida Guinga, com a voz grave, profunda e quase etérea, nos versos iniciais de “Claro da lua”, single que Leo Tomassini lançará em 1º de dezembro.

Tomassini também canta a valsa lírica que compôs por volta de 2007 ou 2008, mas, devoto de Guinga, preferia nem ter posto voz na música gravada com produção musical e o toque do violão de Jean Charnaux.

“Minha ideia inicial e sonho era ter a voz de Guinga do início ao fim. Queria ter minha obra cantada por essa voz mágica. Não há cantor ou cantora no mundo melhor que Guinga. Há tão bons quanto, Chet Baker, João Gilberto, Billie Holiday, Ella Fitzgerald, Gal... Lamento estar ao lado dele nessa faixa. Sinto-me uma cantora dessas muitas que por aí vão atravancando nosso caminho, cheias de assepsias técnicas e zero calor e vida. Tudo na voz de Guinga ganha uma densidade e intenção naturais, o que se canta é vivido”, caracteriza um embevecido Leo Tomassini, cantor e compositor carioca revelado como vocalista da Família Roitman, banda carioca que esteve cena de 1989 a 2003 com nome inspirado no clã disfuncional da novela “Vale tudo” (1988).

Em carreira solo desde 2003, ano em que lançou o álbum “Amor e cordas”, Leo Tomassini aguarda a edição do terceiro álbum solo em 2027, “Jaula de gorila”, gravado sob direção musical do guitarrista Pedro Sá.

Inteiramente autoral, o repertório do álbum “Jaula de gorila” é composto pelas músicas “45 km” (Leo Tomassini e Chacal), “Álcool gel” (Leo Tomassini), “Baião das estrelas” (Leo Tomassini e Mauro Aguiar), “Fim” (Leo Tomassini e Beto Valente), “Gravidade” (Leo Tomassini), “Luz versus luz” (Leo Tomassini a partir de versos de Paulo Leminski), “Pop Cacaso Pop” (Leo Tomassini a partir de versos de Cacaso), “Rápido e rasteiro” (Leo Tomassini e Chacal), “Rapunzel” (Leo Tomassini), “Rei do vermelho e o negro” (Leo Tomassini e Joaquim Tomassini), “Sobre a existência de Deus” (Leo Tomassini) e “Uma voz” (Leo Tomassini a partir de versos de Ferreira Gullar), além da música-título “Jaula de gorila” (Leo Tomassini e Cabelo).

Valsa que Tomassini assina com Jean Charnaux e com o filho Joaquim Tomassini, ambos creditados como autores da composiçãporque cada um sugeriu a mudança de uma nota da melodia, “Claro da lua” não faz parte do repertório do álbum “Jaula de gorila”.

No entanto, a devoção a Guinga conecta o vindouro single avulso viabilizado pela Vogas Produções com o ainda inédito álbum gravado com produção orquestrada por Leo Tomassini com Beno Ibeas e Pedro Sá. A música que encerra o álbum, “Fim”, tem letra arrematada com o verso “Escrevi no chão com tinta: eu te amo, Guinga”.

articles.body:
Música ao vivo e gastronomia são um casamento perfeito para quem procura um final de semana diferente — Foto: Secom

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Quatro dias de gastronomia e música brasileira vão movimentar a região da Boca da Barra, em Rio das Ostras. De 26 a 29 de novembro, a Praia do Cemitério recebe a 27ª edição do Festival de Frutos do Mar, que neste ano tem como tema “Maré Musical Brasileira”. O evento reúne 16 participações de estabelecimentos locais, com receitas inspiradas em artistas, álbuns e canções nacionais, além de apresentações musicais gratuitas.

“O Festival será um grande sucesso porque é tradição na cidade. Contem com o apoio da Administração Municipal porque sabemos que comida é mais que alimento. É cultura e preservação da memória. Esse é um evento do Calendário Oficial que já em sua 27ª Edição. Isso mostra que é um evento consolidado e que mostra a qualidade dos Restaurantes. Justifica também o crescimento da Gastronomia no Município”, disse Rosemarie Teixeira, presidente da Fundação Rio das Ostras de Cultura, que representou o prefeito Carlos Augusto Balthazar.

O Festival de Frutos do Mar será realizado na Praia do Cemitério, na região da Boca da Barra, no Centro de Rio das Ostras. A combinação de gastronomia, música e programação à beira-mar oferece ao público uma oportunidade de conhecer a produção dos estabelecimentos locais e aproveitar atrações culturais durante o fim de semana.

A entrada no festival é gratuita. As entradas gastronômicas custam R$ 28 e os pratos principais, R$ 40. Bebidas e sobremesas terão preços próprios. Na quinta e na sexta-feira, dias 26 e 27, o funcionamento será das 17h à meia-noite. No sábado e no domingo, dias 28 e 29, o público poderá visitar o espaço a partir do meio-dia, também até a meia-noite.

A programação musical começa na quinta, dia 26, às 18h, com Micha e Rodolpho Mendes, seguida pelo show da banda KM 50, às 20h. Na sexta-feira, dia 27, Rafael Spitz se apresenta às 18h e Omnia Vincit, às 20h. No sábado, dia 28, as atrações são Baleias Voadoras, às 15h; cortejo com Ostras Band, às 17h; As Florroseiras, às 18h; e Luan Schuenckel, às 20h. No domingo, dia 29, o Segundo Set Instrumental abre a programação às 14h, seguido por Maycon Melo, às 17h, e Cláudia Falcão, às 19h, que encerra o festival.

“A proposta desta edição é aproximar a culinária da música brasileira. Cada estabelecimento participante criou receitas com nomes ou referências a artistas e obras musicais. O festival não terá competição gastronômica. A iniciativa tem como foco a valorização da gastronomia local e dos sabores do mar”, explicou Jamile Freitas, presidente do Núcleo Gourmet.

O evento é realizado pelo Núcleo Gourmet, em parceria com a Fundação Rio das Ostras de Cultura, e conta com o apoio institucional da Prefeitura de Rio das Ostras e Câmara de Vereadores, além do apoio do Sesc, do Sindicomércio, do Serviço Autônomo de Água e Esgoto - SAAE e da Rio+.
